questions.q: What is human development, and what are its four pillars?

answer.text: Human development is the process of enlarging people's choices and improving their well-being, so that they can lead long, healthy, knowledgeable and comfortable lives. Developed by thinkers such as Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen, it shifts the focus from mere economic growth to the actual lives and freedoms of people, and is measured by the UNDP through the Human Development Index.

Human development rests on four pillars. Equity means making equal opportunities available to everyone, regardless of gender, race or income. Sustainability means meeting the needs of the present without harming the ability of future generations to meet their own. Productivity means raising the output of human labour by investing in people's health and education. Empowerment means giving people, especially the weaker sections, the power to make their own choices and shape their lives.

answer: Together these pillars ensure that development is fair, lasting and truly centred on people.

questions.q: How is human development measured, and what does the Human Development Index show?

answer.text: is the process of enlarging people's choices and freedoms, and it is measured by the Human Development Index (HDI).

list: The HDI combines three basic dimensions of a decent life
These are a long and healthy life, knowledge, and a decent standard of living

answer.text: The index turns them into a single figure.

list: Life expectancy measures health, years of schooling measure knowledge, and per capita income measures living standards
The HDI ranks countries from 0 to 1, showing that development is about people, not only wealth

questions.q: What are the different approaches to human development?

answer.text: can be understood through several approaches, each stressing a different aspect of improving human life.

list: The income approach sees development as a rise in income, on the view that higher income widens choices
The welfare approach sees people as beneficiaries and stresses government spending on health, education and welfare

answer.text: They focus on people's own capacities.

list: The basic needs approach identifies minimum needs — food, water, shelter, health, education — to be provided to all
The capability approach, linked to Amartya Sen, stresses building people's capabilities and freedoms to live as they value
